sections.h2: Quick ways to sell in San Juan
sections.html:
San Juan sellers typically pick among three routes: an agent, a sale on their own, or a cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands. Cash moves fastest. An agent listing can earn the highest price if the house shows well.

The city sits in south central Hidalgo County on Farm Road 1426 and State Highway Spur 374, about six miles northeast of McAllen. Its school district, Pharr-San Juan-Alamo, shows how closely the three towns are tied together. Population grew from 10,815 in 1992 to 26,229 in 2000, so many houses are fairly recent. Keep receipts and records for repairs you have made, because they help a buyer trust the work.

Whatever offer you are weighing, pin down three things: what it assumes about repairs, who pays recording and title costs, and the closing date. Written answers let you hold offers side by side.

The Pharr-San Juan-Alamo Independent School District, established on March 24, 1919, took in all of the schools in San Juan. Check your tax bill for the district listed on your parcel.

On the Hidalgo County Appraisal District website you will find a property search, an online portal for filing exemptions and appeals, and a homestead portal for homestead and over 65 applications. You can reach the district's customer service line at 956-381-8466.

  • Use the property search to see your value, owner and tax history.
  • Use the portal to file an exemption or an appeal.
  • Use the truth in taxation site to see proposed rates from each taxing unit.
  • Use the Comptroller's taxpayer pamphlet for the protest process.

Your bill and the exact rate for each unit come from the county tax office.

The City of San Juan Planning Department handles land use, zoning, permits, subdivisions and rezoning. Its Health, Building and Code Enforcement divisions watch zoning, safety and health rules. The office is at 512 S. Nebraska Ave., and the phone is 956-223-2220.

The city's interactive GIS map shows zoning and city limits. It also tells you whether a location falls under Hidalgo County Precinct 1 or 2 for services outside city jurisdiction, and it helps you work out whether you need city permits or utilities.

If your lot is near the edge of town, begin with a call to this office. Whether a parcel sits inside city limits changes who regulates a garage conversion, an addition or a fence. It is also the place to ask whether a permit is on file for earlier work, a question buyers raise.

The Virgen de San Juan del Valle Shrine, built in 1954, has drawn pilgrims and tourists for decades, and a new shrine was dedicated in April 1980. The city is also known as home of the Bougainvillea Trail of Texas. Visitor traffic gives the city a steady identity, though it does not set your price. When you describe the house, name your block, its distance to schools and the shrine, and any recent work.

Tax bills come in the fall. A bill not paid by February 1 counts as delinquent.

How Texas delinquent tax penalties build up
WhenPenalty or interest
February 1Six percent penalty and one percent interest
Each month until July 1Penalty continues to rise one percent a month; interest is one percent a month
July 1Penalty becomes 12 percent
After attorney referralUp to 20 percent more if the unit has an attorney contract

A written request to waive penalty and interest has to be filed before the 181st day after the delinquency date. Installment plans of up to 36 months exist at some collectors and are required only for a residence homestead.

Each January 1 the tax lien attaches to the property. Any balance still open is normally paid out of what you receive at the closing table. An open bill can slow a sale but need not block it. The county tax office can give you a payoff figure, which your title company then builds into the settlement. If a payment plan is running, say so, so the right balance gets quoted.

A little preparation shortens any sale. Pull your parcel up in the Hidalgo County Appraisal District property search and note the value, owner name and tax history. If you filed an exemption or an appeal through the portal, keep the confirmation. If you hold a homestead or over 65 exemption, tell your buyer, because the new owner has to apply on their own. Gather receipts for roof, drainage and electrical work, and ask the city planning office whether permits were filed for any addition, garage conversion or fence. A buyer who sees permits and receipts up front has fewer reasons to lower the bid.

  • Photo ID and the recorded deed.
  • Newest tax bill, plus a payoff figure from the county tax office.
  • Repair receipts and permit records.
  • Names of any tenants and a copy of the lease.

If the appraised value looks too high, you can protest it. The appraisal district portal accepts appeals online, and the Comptroller's taxpayer pamphlet explains the protest process. The truth in taxation site shows the rates each taxing unit has proposed, so you can see how value and rate combine on your bill. A lower value helps a buyer, and it can help you if you still own the house when the bill arrives.

Deeds for San Juan land go to the Hidalgo County Clerk, and the signer must appear before a notary or other authorized officer.

Inherited houses start with the will, which can be probated up to four years after the death. If liens on the land are the estate's only debts, a muniment of title is one way to put the house in the heirs' names. A title company can tell the heirs which paper a buyer's lender will take.

A tenant complicates timing. Getting a tenant out takes a written notice and then a justice court case. Selling with the tenant in place skips that process and keeps rent coming until closing.

sections.h2: Foreclosure and houses needing major work
sections.html:
Foreclosure in Texas is usually nonjudicial and ends in a public auction. A sale before that date can protect your equity, and excess proceeds after an auction go to junior liens before the former owner.

Houses that need a new roof, drainage work or electrical repairs fit an as is buyer, who absorbs the work. In return you accept a lower price and skip the contractors and the repair requests.

sections.h2: What to expect with a cash sale
sections.html: A cash sale here goes in stages. Step one is a walk-through, after which the buyer names a price. Once you accept, the title company opens a file and searches for liens, including taxes. Next you choose a closing date, sign at the title company's office and collect the proceeds. With no buyer loan involved, nobody waits on a lender's appraisal. Take a photo ID and your deed along, and ask to see the settlement statement before the day itself.

faqs.q: What school district is San Juan in?
faqs.a: The Pharr-San Juan-Alamo Independent School District, established in 1919, took in all of the schools in San Juan. Your tax bill confirms it for your parcel.

faqs.q: Who appraises property in San Juan?
faqs.a: Hidalgo County Appraisal District, which runs a property search plus an online portal for exemptions and appeals. Call 956-381-8466 for help.

faqs.q: Does San Juan have a planning office I can call about permits?
faqs.a: Yes. The Planning and Zoning department handles permits, zoning and rezoning at 956-223-2220. Its GIS map helps you check city limits and zoning.

faqs.q: When do unpaid taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: February 1 for most bills, which is when the six percent penalty and one percent interest begin. The 12 percent penalty arrives July 1.

faqs.q: Can an unpaid tax bill stop a San Juan sale?
faqs.a: Usually not. Any balance is paid from your proceeds at closing, and the county tax office can quote the payoff.
